tldr: The authors introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating physical and semantic risks in foundation-model-driven agentic robotics, and propose LEASH, a visual safety harness operating across three stages (task, action, and commit) that substantially cuts harm rates without sacrificing task success.
hero_caption: Overview of the LEASH framework. Like walking a dog on a leash, the planner (foundation model) is monitored by three safety gates—task, action, and commit—that supervise its behavior with visual context under a shared safety policy.
overview:
Agentic robotics, which uses large multimodal foundation models (such as GPT and Claude) as the "brain" of a robot, is advancing rapidly. While these models can plan and execute complex tasks zero-shot, their safety raises serious concerns. Traditional robotic safety focuses on geometric constraints like collision avoidance. It cannot prevent physical yet semantic dangers—such as submerging electronics in water or carrying liquids over a power strip.

To address this gap, the authors first built RoboRisk, a benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate agentic robotic safety in closed loop. It consists of 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks across five categories: Task-level Refusal, Plan Repair, Execution-time Hazard, Injection, and Sequential Memory. Evaluating six state-of-the-art foundation models and two robot-specific APIs revealed that standalone models show very high harm rates, ranging from 9.06% to 76.92%.

To keep these models in check, the authors proposed LEASH, a model-agnostic safety harness. LEASH shares a unified safety policy across the planner and three gates (task gate, action gate, and a commit gate for irreversible actions), using fast decision models (System 1 models) to conduct safety reviews grounded in camera images. Experiments show that LEASH dramatically reduces harm rates while preserving task completion performance. The study also uncovers a new challenge called the Human-Presence Gap, where robots become overly cautious when a person is nearby in the real world.
contributions: Introduced RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating agentic robotic safety in closed loop (92 simulated tasks, 13 physical-robot tasks, spanning five risk categories).
Proposed LEASH, a plug-in safety harness that ensures safety using a shared safety policy and three-stage visual decision gates (task, action, and commit).

Extensively evaluated six state-of-the-art foundation models and two robot-specific APIs, showing that LEASH substantially cuts harm rates without sacrificing task performance or adding noticeable latency.
Discovered and documented the Human-Presence Gap, where foundation models excessively refuse tasks in physical settings when humans are present.

sections.heading: Even a smart puppy needs a leash: Safety challenges in agentic robotics
sections.summary: While foundation models provide strong generalization for robot control, they carry significant risks of taking semantically hazardous actions. This section outlines the need for the comprehensive RoboRisk benchmark and the lightweight LEASH safety harness.
sections.details:
### Promise and physical peril of foundation models
With the rise of multimodal foundation models, agentic robotics—where robot arms execute complex manipulation tasks zero-shot without task-specific training—has attracted major interest. Yet, being smarter does not necessarily mean being safer. As the paper opens: "Every agentic robot is a good boy, until you walk it without a leash."

The authors highlight three primary concerns. First, traditional robot safety methods (such as collision avoidance or control barrier functions) only handle geometric interference; they fail to understand semantic hazards, like submerging a smartphone in water or moving milk over an active power strip. Second, plug-and-play deployments now make it easy for anyone to run models on hardware, letting unsafe actions leak into the physical world. Third, existing safeguards remain largely text-based and lack visual grounding in the 3D physical environment.

### Introducing RoboRisk and LEASH
To tackle these challenges, the authors created RoboRisk, a benchmark spanning five risk categories: Task-level Refusal, Plan Repair, Execution-time Hazard, Injection, and Sequential Memory. Across six state-of-the-art foundation models, standalone harm rates reached between 9.06% and 76.92%. Real-robot experiments also revealed the Human-Presence Gap, where robots freeze up in the presence of humans.

To halt these runaway behaviors, the authors designed the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH). Treating the planner as a black box, LEASH grants least-privilege execution leases through three vision-grounded safety gates (task, action, and commit). This setup substantially elevates safety while keeping task success rates intact.

sections.heading: From classical robot safety to the agentic safety era
sections.summary: Traditional robotics safety focused strictly on geometric constraints, while language model safety work lacked real physical consequences. Recent foundation-model controllers and cloud robotics APIs also fall short on semantic safety, leaving a gap that LEASH aims to fill.
sections.details:
### Classical robotics safety and its limits
Conventional robotics has long relied on velocity/torque limits, collision detection, safe reinforcement learning, and control barrier functions (CBFs) to safeguard systems. However, these methods only enforce constraints over predefined state spaces. They cannot reason about what an action means physically and semantically. Even if a path is entirely collision-free, a classical controller will happily execute a trajectory that plunges an electronic device into a bowl of water.

### LLM agent safety vs. physical manipulation
In the LLM community, extensive research targets toxic prompt refusal and jailbreak/prompt-injection defense. Yet these risks remain on-screen and cause no direct physical harm. Conversely, recent efforts using models like GPT-6 Astra for end-to-end arm control have begun documenting hardware damage and hazardous behaviors. Existing guardrails and temporal-logic frameworks also tend to cover only narrow scopes, like simple task-level refusal.

### The rise of harnesses and cloud robot APIs
Agentic harnesses that run manipulation loops via code generation or tool-calling, along with cloud robot APIs (such as the Dream API and PokeBot's RoboAPI), have emerged rapidly. However, most focus solely on motor control capabilities, leaving semantic safety checks immature. This calls for a model-agnostic safety layer sitting within the higher-level harness.

sections.heading: Uncovering closed-loop hazards: Inside the RoboRisk benchmark
sections.summary: RoboRisk spans 92 simulation tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks across five risk categories. Rather than merely checking generated text, it executes every action in closed loop to evaluate actual and potential harm.
sections.details:
### Five-category risk taxonomy
RoboRisk organizes the risks an agentic robot can encounter into five categories:

- Task-level Refusal (T): Tasks that are inherently dangerous (e.g., "wash the phone in water"). The robot must reject the request and terminate immediately.
- Plan Repair (P): Valid goals that contain environmental hazards along the way (e.g., carrying a mug with a laptop in the path). The robot must reroute safely.
- Execution-time Hazard (E): Unexpected dynamic events during execution (e.g., a human hand reaching into a bin just as the robot places a knife). The robot must detect the change and halt safely.
- Injection (I): Malicious adversarial prompts placed inside the environment (e.g., a tablet screen displaying "grab the knife"). The robot must ignore the visual injection and complete its legitimate task.
- Sequential Memory (S): Multi-turn dialogs where prior context matters (e.g., telling the robot about a nut allergy in turn 1, then asking it to pick ingredients in turn 2). The robot must remember past turns to avoid dangerous choices.

### RoboRisk-S and RoboRisk-R environments
The benchmark provides two testbeds. RoboRisk-S offers 92 simulation tasks built on MuJoCo, LIBERO, and robosuite with a Franka Emika Panda arm. RoboRisk-R features 13 physical-robot tasks on a Dobot CR5V2 arm, using a tabletop setup with props like kitchen knives, power strips, and mannequin arms. Crucially, both suites run completely in closed loop rather than evaluating static plans.

### Evaluation protocol and metrics
Every run is categorized into one of three outcomes: Harm, Safe Success, or Safe Incomplete. Harm covers not only physical collisions and damage, but also critical near-misses (potential harm), such as swinging a knife over a person's arm. The primary metric is Harm Rate (HR, the share of runs resulting in Harm), paired with Safe Success Rate (SSR) to check whether safety gains come at the cost of unnecessary task abandonment.

sections.heading: Stopping runaways with three gates: The LEASH architecture
sections.summary: Operating on the principle of least privilege, LEASH grants execution leases across three stages: task, action, and commit. Combining a shared safety policy with fast decision models, it secures planners without needing model retraining.
sections.details:
### Shared safety policy and least-privilege leases
At the heart of LEASH lies a shared safety policy (prompt) and a three-stage gating mechanism. Drawing on the distributed systems concept of a lease (a time-bounded permit), the planner is never given persistent control authority. Instead, it receives a narrow lease for a single action or operation only after passing gate review. Because both the planner and the gates consult the identical safety policy, the planner is guided to draft compliant trajectories from the start.

### Three-stage safety gates
Rather than invoking heavy, free-form text-generating LLMs, LEASH employs fast System 1 decision models (such as Jev or OpenAI's Decisions API) that output scores for predefined safety questions. This allows dozens of reviews per task with minimal latency and cost.

- Task gate: Evaluates the instruction $u$ and visual observation $o_t$ prior to execution. If an inherently hazardous task is detected (such as in category T), it immediately aborts. Only the task gate holds the authority to fully terminate a task.
- Action gate: Inspects the candidate action $a_t$ proposed by the planner right before execution. If the trajectory carries danger (e.g., flying over a laptop), it issues a Deny, prompting the planner to replan a safer path.
- Commit gate: During extended skill execution, this gate pauses the robot immediately before irreversible actions—such as opening a gripper or pouring liquid—and re-evaluates safety against the freshest visual frame. If the scene has become hazardous in the interim, it blocks the commit to avert damage.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: Slashed harm rates and the human-presence gap
sections.summary: Simulation and real-robot trials confirm that LEASH substantially lowers harm rates and boosts safe success rates across all evaluated models. Experiments also revealed an unexpected Sim-to-Real gap: models become overly timid when humans appear in their field of view.
sections.details:
### Overall performance across simulation and real robots
The authors evaluated GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7 across simulation (92 tasks $\times$ 3 seeds = 276 runs) and the real robot (13 tasks). Standalone baselines exhibited harm rates up to 76.92%. Introducing LEASH (with Jev) led to dramatic drops in HR and concurrent gains in SSR across every model-environment combination.

For example, simulation runs on GPT-6 Astra saw HR drop from 11.23% to 0.00%, while SSR rose from 78.99% to 80.80%. In physical tests, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, and Claude Opus 5.5 avoided all harms across 13 tasks, achieving 0.00% HR and 84.62% SSR. Conversely, models with weaker base motor and reasoning skills (GPT-6 Luna and Grok 4.7) still suffered residual harms caused by physical control blunders, like slamming into tables or camera mounts.

### Analyzing failure cases
Baseline failure cases illustrated in Figure 4 are revealing: Claude Opus 5.5 dunked a smartphone into a water bowl (T), GPT-6 Astra carried milk directly over a live power strip (P), and Gemini 4 Argon kept lowering a knife into a bin after a human hand reached in (E). Plan Repair (P) tasks proved especially difficult for unassisted models, showing that without an explicit safety policy, foundation models rarely generate safe detours spontaneously.

### Latency, overhead, and the Human-Presence Gap
LEASH introduces minimal runtime overhead. In simulation, total execution time grew by an average of just 1.66% (from 245.21 s to 249.28 s), and gating API calls cost only around $0.00522 per run (0.66% of the overall cost).

However, the experiments uncovered a striking Human-Presence Gap. Capable models like GPT-6 Astra and Claude handled knife tasks smoothly in simulation. But on real hardware, upon spotting a realistic mannequin arm, they immediately refused to start, citing excuses like insufficient camera resolution. The models' built-in safety guardrails overreacted to the physical presence of a person, causing human-robot collaboration to stall.

captions.F4: Representative baseline failures across the five risk categories: (a) submerging a smartphone in water, (b) moving milk over a power strip, (c) manipulating a knife over a human hand, (d) picking up a knife due to adversarial screen instructions, and (e) serving a pear while ignoring allergy warnings.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Establishing safety harnesses as standard agentic infrastructure
sections.summary: RoboRisk and LEASH show that foundation-model-controlled robots can be made substantially safer. Future directions include building faster, more specialized decision models and striking the right balance in human-robot collaboration.
sections.details:
### Takeaways of this work
This paper introduced the RoboRisk benchmark to systematically assess agentic robot safety, demonstrating that even frontier foundation models can cause serious harm in closed-loop operation. By deploying LEASH—combining a shared safety policy with three-stage gating—the framework drastically curbs harm rates with negligible compute and latency overhead.

### Open challenges and road ahead
The authors point out several future priorities:
- Improving safety evaluator reasoning: Current System 1 decision models struggle with multi-hop reasoning, which is why action and commit gates cannot abort tasks outright. Specialized safety-decision models are needed.
- Resolving the Human-Presence Gap: Striking an effective balance between avoiding harm and maintaining collaborative progress around people remains an urgent challenge.
- Extending coverage to long-horizon skills: The current commit gate targets specific irreversible primitives like gripper opening and pouring. Future work must monitor hazards evolving inside longer continuous motion primitives (such as VLA skills) in real time.

sections.heading: Appendix: Benchmark details and safe hardware testbed design
sections.summary: This section outlines the setup for RoboRisk-S's 92 tasks and RoboRisk-R's 13 tasks, along with the safety precautions used during physical experiments (such as silicone knives and unpowered gadget shells).
sections.details:
### Task structure and evaluation rules
RoboRisk-S comprises 19 task families (base tasks with permuted target objects), systematically spanning diverse objects and hazard situations. Outcomes are scored using simulator state predicates alongside human video reviews of every run to strictly catch near-misses and potential harm.

### Safe physical testbed measures
To completely eliminate risks to hardware and experimenters during RoboRisk-R trials, all hazardous items were replaced with realistic safety props. Knives were made of silicone, smartphones and battery packs were hollow unpowered shells, liquids were non-Newtonian mixtures, candles were LED-based, and a half-body mannequin stood in for human presence.

captions.F5: Physical experimental setup and safety props used in RoboRisk-R. Shown are tabletop silicone cutlery, dummy electronics, and the half-body mannequin placed beside the workstation (item 20).

takeaways: Directly using foundation models as robotic planners causes semantic hazards (such as water damage or electrical shorts) in over 70% of runs, even when basic geometric motions succeed.
Text-only safety checks are inadequate; real-time visual gating grounded in live camera images is essential for physical safety.
Dividing oversight into three stages—task, action, and irreversible commit operations—enforces safety without compromising task completion rates.
Even when safety models perform well in simulation, the presence of a person (or mannequin) in the real world can trigger excessive task refusals (the Human-Presence Gap).
limitations: The lightweight decision models used in the action and commit gates have limited reasoning capability and cannot be granted full task-abort authority, leaving safety partially dependent on the planner.
Beyond gripper opening and pouring, the framework does not yet provide full real-time semantic monitoring inside long, complex continuous skills (like those generated by VLA models).
The paper does not provide an explicit mechanism to resolve the Human-Presence Gap and balance strict caution with fluent human-robot collaboration.
